section_summary: This section documents U.S. monitoring of Japanese diplomatic, commercial, propaganda, broadcasting, and intelligence activity across Latin America during 1940–1941. It includes reports on Japanese economic countermeasures, the travel of military attachés and other nationals, repatriation from South America, alleged arms and espionage networks, and propaganda directed at Latin American audiences. The section ends with a Bogotá despatch and extracts from the Buenos Aires magazine Oriente y Occidente, illustrating the cultural and political content of Japanese overseas propaganda.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese activities in Costa Rica
subfiles.about: References a report that a Japanese shipping company wished to acquire German and Italian merchant ships sheltering in Western Hemisphere ports.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references the original Costa Rican despatch. It states that the vessels would be used between Japanese, Russian, and American ports.

subfiles.title: Circular on anticipated economic pressure against Japan
subfiles.to: All American diplomatic and consular officers in the American republics
subfiles.about: Distributes intelligence on Japanese plans to counter expected U.S. and British economic pressure in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed November 23 memorandum says Tokyo anticipated financial restrictions, obstruction of trade treaties, raw-material embargoes, and difficulties at the Panama Canal. Japanese representatives were instructed to seek banking or barter arrangements, conduct trade talks secretly, secure supply promises, and promote free-transit agitation concerning the canal. Pages 85–86 duplicate the instruction and memorandum.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for an enclosure
subfiles.about: Records the temporary charging or removal of an enclosure from file 894.20210.
subfiles.summary: The sheet is an administrative file-control record. Its handwritten notation is largely illegible and supplies no substantive intelligence.

subfiles.title: Transmission concerning attempts to buy South American tungsten
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards an FBI letter about alleged Japanese and German efforts to purchase all available tungsten in South America.
subfiles.summary: Price transmits a confidential January 2 FBI communication for the administrator’s information. The reported purchasing effort involved both Japanese and German interests.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese radio broadcasts to Latin America
subfiles.about: References a Brazilian despatch reporting new Japanese broadcasts in Portuguese, Spanish, and Japanese.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to despatch no. 3084. Its subject is the inauguration of Tokyo broadcasts beamed toward Latin America.

subfiles.title: Japanese propaganda activities in Brazil: daily radio broadcasts
subfiles.from: William C. Burdett, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese shortwave broadcasts aimed at Latin America and an honor granted to President Vargas.
subfiles.summary: Burdett reports that the Tokyo broadcaster began daily Portuguese-, Spanish-, and Japanese-language transmissions on December 11, listing call signs, frequencies, and times. He also notes reports that the Japanese emperor had awarded President Vargas the Grand Cordon of the Order of the Chrysanthemum.

subfiles.title: Departmental summary of reported Japanese departures from Peru
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Lima despatch alleging that Japanese residents had been told to leave Peru.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says Japanese residents were rumored to have been directed to return to Japan within three months or remain at their own risk. It notes that Japanese ships had carried many nationals home and argues that the departures cast doubt on claims of a militarized Japanese colony in Peru.

subfiles.title: Reported departure of Japanese from Peru upon direction of the Japanese government
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Lima; signed J. F. McGurk
subfiles.about: Reports rumors that Japanese citizens in Peru were being ordered home within three months.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese resident reportedly confirmed receiving such a notice, though its precise issuing authority was unknown. Peruvian officials said Japanese ships had recently carried many residents away and speculated that Japan might become more active in the international conflict. The embassy concluded that a mass departure would undermine rumors of a Japanese military colony prepared for action in South America.

subfiles.title: Inquiry concerning the travel of Japanese naval attachés
subfiles.doc_type: outgoing telegram with handwritten follow-up note
subfiles.about: Advises that Ichiro Yokoyama and Yuzuru Sanematsu obtained visas for travel to Mexico, Guatemala, and Panama.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports that the Japanese naval attaché and assistant naval attaché were preparing an early journey through the three countries. A handwritten follow-up seeks confirmation of Sanematsu’s and Yokoyama’s movements, apparently through San Francisco, Miami, and Havana.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting Sanematsu’s return from Panama
subfiles.about: Reports that Yuzuru Sanematsu would arrive in Miami from Panama on February 11.
subfiles.summary: The telegram answers the Department’s February 6 inquiry about the Japanese assistant naval attaché. It states briefly that Sanematsu was traveling by air from Panama to Miami.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on non-American activities in Bolivia
subfiles.about: References a report on non-American activities in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs the reader to the original despatch in another decimal file. It contains no substantive details beyond the subject, origin, and filing reference.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on a Japanese economic mission
subfiles.about: References a report on a Japanese economic mission planning to visit Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, and Venezuela.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies the mission’s proposed South American itinerary. It points to despatch no. 3898 in another file.

subfiles.title: Expected arrival of a Japanese economic mission
subfiles.from: William C. Burdett, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports that a Japanese economic mission would leave Japan aboard the Montevideo Maru for four South American countries.
subfiles.summary: The announced mission was to visit Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, and Venezuela. Burdett comments that almost every ship arriving from Japan appeared to carry some kind of mission.

subfiles.title: FBI letter concerning a Tokyo message to Havana
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidentially obtained message sent from Tokyo to the Norddeutscher Lloyd office in Havana concerning a travel reservation.
subfiles.summary: The badly degraded quoted message appears to request information about an unanswered reservation originating at Balboa. Copies were supplied to naval and military intelligence officials.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese crews at Puntarenas
subfiles.about: References a report about increasing numbers of Japanese crewmen on American tuna boats at Puntarenas.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies the subject and source despatch. The original was filed under a separate fisheries-related number.

subfiles.title: FBI letter and memorandum on Japanese and German travel
subfiles.about: Provides confidential information on the movements of Japanese and German travelers in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure lists journeys involving Sueji Yagi, several Germans, the Huelsberg family, Keiichiro Kusutani, and Kokichi Suzuki. Routes connect Ecuador, Colombia, Central America, Venezuela, Mexico, Texas, and New Orleans, and one German traveler was reportedly employed by Meredith Nicholson.

subfiles.title: Continuation of military attaché report on Japanese and German plans
subfiles.doc_type: military attaché report continuation and file sheet
subfiles.from: Ralph H. Wooten, U.S. Military Attaché in Chile
subfiles.about: Relays an informant’s claims about Japanese arms, German separatist plans, and Axis strategy in the Americas and Pacific.
subfiles.summary: The report alleges that Japanese interests were accumulating arms in Brazil and especially Peru through concealed cargo, floating boxes, and coastal landings. It also describes alleged German designs on southern Chile and Japanese expectations of war with the United States, seizure of the Philippines and Australia, accommodation with Russia, and sabotage of the Panama Canal. Page 106 is an otherwise blank file-number sheet associated with the report.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on conferences concerning Latin America
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese government conferences on Latin American problems and alleged mistreatment of Japanese residents.
subfiles.summary: A Domei report said Foreign Office, communications, army, navy, and planning officials were discussing Latin American policy. It alleged oppression of 200,000 Japanese residents through the U.S. Pan-American campaign and consideration of measures against obstruction of Japanese trade and emigration.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese subversive activities
subfiles.about: References an FBI report on German and Japanese nationals traveling in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: The sheet classifies the material under Japanese subversive activities in America. It points to the original Department of Justice letter in another file.

subfiles.title: FBI report on the Japanese military attaché’s movement
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese military attaché in Mexico City left Guatemala City for Panama.
subfiles.summary: The information confirmed a May 1 telephone conversation between Fletcher Warren and S. J. Drayton. A reliable source dated the attaché’s departure to April 29, 1941.

subfiles.title: Instruction concerning Rafael Espinosa
subfiles.about: Reports allegations that Rafael Espinosa was a smuggler, narcotics dealer, and Nazi agent corresponding with the German Legation.
subfiles.summary: Espinosa, a Colombian living near the Canal Zone, had reportedly once advised Colombia on smuggling from Panama. The Department asked the embassy to treat the information strictly confidentially; a parallel instruction went to Panama.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Panama concerning Toshiaki Nishi
subfiles.about: Requests information on Japanese military attaché Toshiaki Nishi’s activities in Panama.
subfiles.summary: The Department reports that Nishi had reserved extensive travel through Central and South America and left Guatemala City for Panama on April 29. It asks the embassy to observe and report on his activities.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Guatemala concerning Toshiaki Nishi
subfiles.about: Requests information on Toshiaki Nishi’s activities while in Guatemala.
subfiles.summary: The instruction repeats that the Japanese military attaché had arranged broad travel through Central and South America. It notes his April 29 departure for Panama and says a parallel request was sent there.

subfiles.title: Continuation of report on alleged Japanese war plans
subfiles.about: Repeats claims about Japanese plans in the Philippines, Australia, China, and the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: The fragment says Japan expected to defeat the Philippines, take Australia, reach an agreement with Russia over China, and close the Panama Canal with bombs attached to ships. An informer adds that incendiary raids, hunger, domestic opposition, and anti-Japanese Korean workers could cause Japan to collapse.

subfiles.title: Extract on Japanese propaganda funds for El Salvador’s consul
subfiles.to: State Department and military intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Reports that El Salvador’s consul in Tokyo received Japanese money for propaganda in Central America.
subfiles.summary: French intelligence in Hong Kong reportedly learned that the consul received 100,000 yen in 1936. The source alleged that he remained in Japan and continued distributing Japanese funds for the same purpose.

subfiles.title: Instruction to San Salvador on propaganda by its Tokyo consul
subfiles.about: Asks for information and comment about alleged Japanese propaganda activities by El Salvador’s consul in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The Department reports that the consul received substantial Japanese funds in 1936 and later distributed additional money. The minister is requested to investigate and submit his assessment.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo on propaganda by El Salvador’s consul
subfiles.about: Requests information about the alleged Japanese propaganda activities of El Salvador’s consul in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The instruction repeats allegations that the consul received substantial funds in 1936 and later dispensed more Japanese money. The ambassador is asked to report any relevant information and comments.

subfiles.title: Extended trip of the Japanese military attaché through Central and South America
subfiles.from: Merton H. McCoy, U.S. Military Attaché, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports Toshiaki Nishi’s planned itinerary through Central and South America.
subfiles.summary: Pan American Airways supplied reservations taking Nishi from Mexico City through Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Argentina, Brazil, Trinidad, Venezuela, and back toward Mexico. McCoy argues that visits outside Colombia and Venezuela, where Nishi was accredited, warranted particular observation. The report emphasizes long stays in Panama, Bogotá, Lima, Buenos Aires, Rio de Janeiro, and La Guaira.

subfiles.title: FBI confirmation of Nishi’s Belém–Port of Spain reservation
subfiles.about: Reports an airline reservation probably made by Toshiaki Nishi from Belém to Port of Spain.
subfiles.summary: A reliable source said a person recorded as “Nihhi,” probably Japanese, reserved air travel for June 20. Copies went to naval and military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Consul for El Salvador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the resignation of León Sigüenza after allegations that he handled Japanese propaganda funds.
subfiles.summary: Frazer says similar information had already reached him through U.S. naval intelligence and that he discreetly informed a senior Salvadoran official. El Salvador’s official gazette then announced acceptance of Sigüenza’s resignation as consul general in Japan and cancellation of his exequatur.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding report of the Salvadoran consul’s resignation
subfiles.about: Forwards the San Salvador despatch reporting the resignation of El Salvador’s consul general in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The instruction recalls the May 12 inquiry into the consul’s alleged Japanese propaganda work. It encloses Robert Frazer’s May 16 report that the consul general had resigned.

subfiles.title: Report on Japanese migration from Peru to Chile or Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese residents might leave Peru because of unemployment and fear, with many expected to enter Chile.
subfiles.summary: A reliable source said Japanese Legation personnel expected a large but unspecified number to leave Peru, about eighty percent of them for Chile. The report alleges they would use three-month tourist visas despite Chilean exclusion laws. It also says Japanese women and children were leaving Peru for Japan in considerable numbers.

subfiles.title: FCC forwarding letter concerning Earl Nicholas
subfiles.about: Forwards Earl Nicholas’s April 8 communication to the commanding officer at Fort Leavenworth.
subfiles.summary: Fly sends the communication for Long’s information. Page 125 is a clean copy of the same forwarding letter.

subfiles.title: Earl Nicholas letter on Japanese radio contacts with South America
subfiles.about: Describes monitoring Japanese broadcasts and point-to-point transmissions directed toward South America and urges interception by U.S. and British forces.
subfiles.summary: Nicholas says he had supplied the British Embassy with frequencies, schedules, reception verifications, and radio guides for Japanese transmissions to Brazil, Argentina, Venezuela, and other destinations. He advocates interception from South American waters or the Canal Zone and claims long-standing correspondence with Axis broadcasters had produced useful propaganda and intelligence material. The letter also comments broadly on FCC monitoring, the war in Europe, and his earlier warnings to democratic governments.

subfiles.title: FBI report on increased Japanese repatriation
subfiles.about: Reports increased repatriation of Japanese nationals, particularly women and children, from South America.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source said the movement had increased considerably. Mitsui and Mitsubishi reportedly instructed the wives and families of company officials to return to Japan.

subfiles.title: British report on Japanese and German activities in South America and the Pacific
subfiles.about: Forwards a British diplomatic telegram containing allegations about Japanese and German ambitions, arms, and war plans.
subfiles.summary: The British telegram relays information from a White Russian in contact with the Japanese Legation in Santiago. It alleges Japanese arms accumulation in Brazil and Peru, German plans for southern Chile, Japanese expectations of war with the United States, and prospective conquests in the Philippines and Australia. It also claims Japan would bargain with Russia over China and could sabotage the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese diplomatic movements through Guatemala
subfiles.about: References a report on Japanese diplomatic officials moving through Guatemala and Central America.
subfiles.summary: The note says the movements had been known to the Foreign Office and U.S. legation for several weeks. It directs the reader to the original document in another file.

subfiles.title: FBI report on diplomatic travel from the Canal Zone
subfiles.about: Reports recent travel by four Japanese diplomats and one German in northern South America and the Canal Zone.
subfiles.summary: Matsumi Kato and Itsuki Takada traveled from Balboa to Medellín, Hiroichi Takagi from Cristóbal to Miami, and Yasutari Hanami from Cristóbal to Quito. Erich Lindner reportedly held reservations between Lima and Quito.

subfiles.title: FBI report on travelers in Latin America
subfiles.about: Lists recent journeys by Japanese and other individuals between Chile, the Canal Zone, Argentina, and Peru.
subfiles.summary: The named travelers were Shingero Ohta, Eizo Mekata, Akira Uesugi, Yoshikiyo Arimori, Akira Uye, and Alberto Westphal. Their movements occurred between July 1 and July 10, 1941.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on a proposed Japanese Diet inspection trip
subfiles.to: American diplomatic officers in the other American republics
subfiles.about: References a circular requesting reports on a proposed South American tour by five members of the Japanese Diet.
subfiles.summary: The proposed travelers were Haruji Tahara, Sobei Hara, Rikure Shinohara, Shigeo Nishimura, and Sotaro Sakamoto. Diplomatic officers were asked to submit any information they could obtain.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese banks and Honduran dollar collections
subfiles.about: References information on an attempt by Japanese banks to centralize dollar collections from other American republics in a Honduran bank.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a financial maneuver involving Japanese banks and Honduras. The original information appears in a despatch filed under frozen credits.

subfiles.title: Analysis of Japanese movements through Central America, January–May 1941
subfiles.doc_type: naval intelligence report with charts and commentary
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese travel through Central America and supplies a traveler index, monthly movement charts, and an intelligence comment.
subfiles.summary: The report finds little Japanese movement until late April, followed by a concentration of diplomats and commercial representatives in Honduras during May. It identifies weaknesses in reporting travel by TACA aircraft and coastal steamers and proposes securing more complete passenger information. The annexes list Japanese travelers, roles, and routes by country and month. A final comment attributes interest in Honduras to an alleged revolutionary plot and to Japanese assistance after Christian Zinsser’s expulsion disrupted German espionage there.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on German port activities and a Japanese mission
subfiles.about: References a report on German activities at ports of call and the views of a Japanese mission.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies George L. Kreeck’s letter and its subject. The original report is filed among records on subversive activities.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Japanese travelers Kagai and Hapa
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese travel from Mexico City to Panama and from Panama to Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: Jux Kagai traveled from Mexico City to Panama City on August 5 using a diplomatic passport. Takeshi Hapa traveled from Panama City to San José on August 3.

subfiles.title: Distribution of Japanese propaganda: Oriente y Occidente
subfiles.about: Forwards issues of a Buenos Aires magazine distributed free in Colombia and identified as Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Braden describes Oriente y Occidente as a monthly magazine resembling the Spanish Reader’s Digest and notes that its nominally paid issues were circulated free in Colombia. The enclosed March 1941 material mixes Japanese culture, Asian strategy, Argentine advertising, and international commentary. Surviving pages include the contents, articles on Buddhist sculpture and Singapore’s naval base, and a literary discussion of Andalusian Arabic poetry.
